title: Israel's EarlySense developed an under-mattress sensor that monitors patients' heart rate and breathing without contact

trailer.text: The company developed a sensor that is placed under the mattress or in a chair cushion and does not need to touch the patient.
The system was intended for patients outside intensive care, whom staff usually check only at set intervals.
According to the company in 2020, the technology was installed in more than 40,000 beds in hospitals and post-acute care facilities.

paragraphs.text: According to NICE, outside intensive care, vital signs are often monitored through checks by nursing staff at set intervals.
According to NICE, if a patient's condition deteriorates between checks, detection of the change may be delayed.
According to a British study summary, in the 24 hours before admission to intensive care, as many as 80% of these patients showed abnormal values for heart rate, breathing rate and oxygenation.
Another danger is falls.
Falls are considered one of the major hazards leading to injuries, complications and even death among hospitalised patients, especially the elderly and people with dementia.
According to a 2007 report by the UK's National Patient Safety Agency, falls account for almost 40% of safety incidents in NHS hospitals.
According to the same report, an average 800-bed acute hospital has over 1,260 falls a year, at an estimated cost of at least £92,000.
Avner Halperin was the company's CEO from its founding.
The company is described as an Israeli digital health startup providing contact-free continuous monitoring solutions.
According to O'Malley, development took about six years, and the sensors were tested on more than 60,000 patients.

stations.title: A notepad-sized sensor, under the mattress

paragraphs.text: According to NICE, it is a contact-free continuous measurement system for routine monitoring of hospital patients outside intensive care.
The system is based on a piezoelectric sensor placed under the mattress or in a chair cushion.
According to O'Malley, the sensor is the size of a pad of legal paper, and it detects vibration through the mattress.
According to the company's announcement, the sensor never touches the patient.
High and low alerts for heart rate and breathing rate can be set for each patient.
According to HealthExec, the InSight system relays the data to a variety of connected devices.
According to the company's announcement, the system was designed for low-risk patients outside intensive care.
According to NICE, the system with Vitals software costs about £35,000 for a 10-bed unit, and the sensor is replaced every year at a cost of £475 per bed, excluding VAT.
According to NICE, the system's components received CE marks in April 2009.
According to NICE, in a case series of 38 intensive care patients, heart rate accuracy was 92.1% and breathing rate accuracy was 80.1%, compared with manual counting.
In Eyal Zimlichman's study, 113 patients were analysed, and nine of them had a major clinical event.
In a study published in the Journal of Hospital Medicine, in predicting deterioration by heart rate, sensitivity was 82% and specificity 67%.
By breathing rate, sensitivity was 64% and specificity 81%.
Zimlichman said the system measured breathing and heart rate continuously, with few alerts.
In Brown's study, in the unit that used the system, code blue events fell from 6.3 to 0.9 per 1,000 patients (p<0.01).
In an internal company report, signs of deterioration were detected in 31 of 35 deterioration events (88.6%).
According to the same internal report, the system detected signs of deterioration in 100% of the major events.
According to a study summarised by NICE, the system can indicate which ventilated patients are not yet ready for extubation.
The study collected 833 patient records at the Dorot Geriatric Center in Netanya, a 374-bed facility.
The study also collected 773 records at the Hebrew Home at Riverdale, an 870-bed skilled nursing facility.
According to HealthExec, the Hebrew Home at Riverdale saw a decrease of nearly 40 percent in falls.
Dr. Zachary Palace said the system alerted to early warning signs of deterioration, the staff responded, and "literally save four lives".
Dr. Gad Mendelson of the Dorot Center said that thanks to the low number of false alarms, the staff reached deteriorating patients earlier, without alarm fatigue.
According to the company, Newton-Wellesley Hospital reported dozens of cases in which InSight alerted staff and helped them care for patients in time.
Nurse Jessie Munn said the sensor detected a low breathing rate in a patient with schizoaffective disorder and cancer who was suffering uncontrollable pain.
According to Munn, the breathing difficulties were linked to a Fentanyl patch, and the patient's condition improved after it was removed.
According to the company's announcement, it was chosen as a framework provider for the supply of fall-prevention products in 34 NHS hospitals, with over 6,000 beds in North West England.
The UK Health Research Authority registered a study examining the impact of the monitoring system on fall prevention in one acute UK hospital.
One of the study's aims is to measure the system's impact on the number and severity of falls.
According to HIT Consultant, in 2016 a $25 million round brought total funding to $100 million, with investments from Samsung, Welch Allyn and Mitsui.
On 7 January 2019, the company announced a $39 million round, mostly from Hill-Rom and Wells Fargo.
According to chairman Itai Harel, within a year the company more than tripled its installations in hospitals and nursing homes.
CEO Avner Halperin claimed that in 2018 alone the technology saved providers over $100 million and prevented 3,000 deaths, 5,000 falls and 4,000 cardiac arrests.
In April 2019 it was reported that Matt Johnson would replace Halperin as CEO.
According to Calcalist, the company's sensors would be used to continuously monitor vital signs of newborns in hospitals in Nairobi, Kenya.
In March 2020 the company announced that Sheba Medical Center was using its system to monitor isolated patients suspected of coronavirus exposure.
According to the company's announcement, the sensor transmits real-time data to a display outside the room.
This way staff need to put on protective clothing and enter isolation areas less often.

stations.title: Questions, criticism and the end of the company

paragraphs.text: According to NICE, the available clinical evidence was limited in quantity and quality.
NICE noted that Brown's study was not truly randomised and was not blinded.
NICE also noted that in this study there was a large difference in intensive care days between the two wards from the start, and that this difference may have caused bias.
Brown's study found no significant differences in transfers to intensive care or in APACHE II scores.
NICE noted that Zimlichman's study recruited patients at increased risk of respiratory failure, so the results may not apply to a general medical ward.
Prof. Robert Wachter, whom the company quotes as supporting the study, is a member of the company's Medical Advisory Board.
Two specialists consulted by NICE were concerned that the upfront cost was too high for the NHS, without clear data on future savings.
Two specialists noted that the system requires patients to be in bed, so its benefit may be limited.
One specialist remarked that "alarm fatigue" is a risk in all early warning systems, when staff ignore alerts because of false alarms.
Nurse Jessie Munn said the system was not integrated with the hospital's communication platform, so staff had to carry multiple alert devices.
According to Calcalist, the company fell into debt and went into receivership.
According to Calcalist, EarlySense sold its intellectual property rights for $30 million.

disagreements.question: By how much did falls decrease with the system?

According to HealthExec, the decrease in falls at the Hebrew Home at Riverdale was nearly 40 percent
According to the company's announcement, Dr. Spiegel of the Dorot Center presented a 28% reduction in falls
According to the same announcement, US researchers reported a 47% decrease in fall events

disagreements.question: What changed in transfers and readmissions at the Dorot Center?

versions.says: According to the company's announcement, transfers to the hospital decreased by 21%, but without statistical significance (p=0.12)
According to the company's announcement, Dr. Spiegel presented a 19% improvement in readmission rates

claims.text: במחקר של בראון לא נמצאו הבדלים מובהקים סטטיסטית בהעברות לטיפול נמרץ או בציוני APACHE II בין שתי המחלקות.
claims.quote: There were no statistically significant differences in ICU transfers or APACHE II scores between the 2 wards after the EarlySense system was introduced.

claims.text: NICE ציין שמחקר זימליכמן גייס מטופלים בסיכון מוגבר לאי ספיקה נשימתית, ולכן התוצאות אולי אינן מתאימות למחלקה פנימית רגילה.
claims.quote: The study recruited patients at an increased risk for respiratory failure, so the results from this study may not be applicable to a general medical ward.

claims.text: פרופ' רוברט וואכטר, שמצטט תומך במחקר, הוא חבר במועצה הרפואית המייעצת של החברה.
claims.quote: a member of the EarlySense Medical Advisory Board

claims.text: שני מומחים שהתייעצו איתם ב-NICE חששו שעלות ההקמה גבוהה מדי ל-NHS ללא נתונים ברורים על חיסכון עתידי.
claims.quote: Two specialist commentators were concerned that the upfront cost of the EarlySense system might be prohibitive for the NHS without clear data on the likely downstream savings

claims.text: שני מומחים ציינו שהמערכת דורשת שהמטופלים יהיו במיטה, ולכן התועלת שלה עלולה להיות מוגבלת.
claims.quote: Two specialist commentators noted that the EarlySense system needed patients to be in bed for monitoring

claims.text: מומחה אחד העיר ש"עייפות מהתראות" היא סיכון במערכות התראה מוקדמת בכלל, כשהצוות מתעלם מהתראות בגלל התראות שווא.
claims.quote: One commentator noted the risk of 'alarm fatigue' from early warning systems in general

claims.text: לפי מאן, המערכת עדיין לא משולבת בפלטפורמת התקשורת הנייחת של בית החולים, ולכן הצוות נאלץ לשאת כמה מכשירי התראה.
claims.quote: Munn said the system is so new that it doesn't yet integrate with the hospital's mobile phone-based nurse-patient care communication platform, forcing clinicians to carry multiple alert devices.

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, החברה שפיתחה חיישנים למיטות בית חולים נקלעה לחובות ונכנסה לכינוס נכסים.
claims.quote: The company, which developed sensors for hospital beds, fell into debt and went into receivership.

claims.text: לפי כלכליסט, ארלי-סנס מכרה את זכויות הקניין הרוחני שלה תמורת 30 מיליון דולר.
claims.quote: Earlysense sells its intellectual property rights for $30 million

claims.text: לפי הודעת החברה, בניסוי בבית אבות בבית ההברי בריוורדייל ירד שיעור הנפילות ב-38.5% (p<0.05).
claims.quote: the falls rate decreased by 38.5% (p<0.05) at the Hebrew Home

claims.text: לפי הודעת החברה, ד"ר ספיגל ממרכז דורות הציג ירידה של 28% בנפילות ושיפור של 19% בשיעורי אשפוז חוזר.
claims.quote: a 28% reduction in falls and a 19% improvement in readmission rates

claims.text: לפי אותה הודעה, חוקרים אמריקאים דיווחו על ירידה של 47% באירועי נפילה בשימוש במערכת.
claims.quote: US researchers reported a 47% decrease of fall events using the EarlySense monitoring solution.

claims.text: לפי הודעת החברה, שיעור ההעברות לבית החולים במרכז דורות ירד ב-21%, אך ללא מובהקות סטטיסטית (p=0.12).
claims.quote: The transfer rate to the hospital decreased by 21% (p=0.12) at Dorot

claims.text: לפי הודעת החברה ב-2013, מטופלים כאלה נבדקים בדרך כלל על ידי הצוות הסיעודי כאחת לארבע שעות בערך.
claims.quote: who are usually monitored by nursing staff approximately once every four hours

claims.text: לפי הודעת החברה ב-2013, מטה החברה נמצא בוולתם, מסצ'וסטס.
claims.quote: EarlySense Inc. is headquartered in Waltham, MA. Investors include: JK&B, Pitango Venture Capital, Etgar Challenge Fund
EarlySense was founded in 2004.
